newsitem.title: LUXEMBOURG: EU studies new fishing reduction compromise.
newsitem.headline: EU studies new fishing reduction compromise.

text.p: European Union fisheries ministers examined a new compromise plan on Tuesday to soften the pain of a proposed fishing cutback to save endangered stocks by extending it over a longer period.

The Dutch EU Presidency suggested that the reduction of up to 30 percent for the most depleted stocks, either in fleet capacity or fishing time at sea, be phased over five years to the end of 2001, instead of over three years.
"Reduction percentages are lower because they are spread over a longer time," Dutch Fisheries Minister Jozias Van Aartsen told reporters as he entered a second day of talks.

The EU's executive Commission originally proposed a 40 percent reduction over six years but this was fiercely rejected by EU member states, fearful of the political backlash if poor fishing communities were thrown out of work.

British Fisheries Minister Tony Baldry reiterated that Britain would not implement any cuts until the vexed question of so-called quota hoppers -- mainly Spanish and Dutch fishermen who buy British fishing licences -- was settled.
"The UK isn't prepared to contemplate any further reduction in its fishing fleet until the whole issue of quota hoppers is dealt with," Baldry told reporters on Tuesday.
Baldry noted that over a quarter of the British national quota was now taken by foreign boats.
"That's grossly unfair on British fishermen and cannot continue," he said, reiterating that Britain would block an inter-governmental conference reviewing the EU Treaty until the problem was solved.
However Dutch minister Van Aartsen said the quota hopper issue was only raised briefly on Monday during the ministerial meeting.

Asked about Britain's stated intention not to implement any further fishing cuts, EU Fisheries Commissioner Emma Bonino responded, "I had understood that the U.K. was a state which abided by the law."
Bonino stressed that ministers were aware of the importance of reaching agreement on Tuesday.
Otherwise the EU will cut off restructuring aid worth hundreds of millions of dollars annually. The aid goes mostly to southern member states and Ireland with many small boats.
